newsitem.title: UK: RBS considers venture with Scottish Widows.
newsitem.headline: RBS considers venture with Scottish Widows.

text.p: Royal Bank of Scotland is in talks with mutually-owned life assurer Scottish Widows, which could lead to Widows taking at least a 20 percent stake in the bank's tied life assurance subsidiary and the joint development of a range of life assurance and long term savings products.

The companies' announcement on Thursday of plans for co-operation follow RBS' agreement with another mutual life assurer Scottish Equitable to end their relationship. Scottish Equitable is to cede its 20 percent share in RBS' life subsidiary Royal Scottish Assurance.
RBS Chief Executive George Mathewson is hopeful of an agreement with Widows in a few weeks. The life assurer is likely to play a wider role with RBS than Scottish Equitable did.

"We're focused at the moment on Royal Scottish Assurance, but we do see the potential for other types of co-operation and so we're building a relationship which will give us a stability and a confidence whereby we can develop other products," said Mathewson in an interview with Reuters.

In addition to providing administrative services for Royal Scottish Assurance and developing a range of products, Widows will also play a crucial role in the expansion of Direct Line Life, the telephone-based life division of RBS.

Widows could, for example, help Direct Line Life to sell pensions over the telephone. At present, the unit sells three protection-only life assurance products -- mortgage protection, term assurance and disability cover.
"They (Scottish Widows) are the only company that we know that has had a successful experience of selling pensions on the telephone," said Mathewson.

Few in the financial services sector have begun to sell pensions over the telephone. Direct Line pioneered telephone-based motor insurance selling in the 1980s and its success at this intensified competition among British insurers.

Some industry experts argue the complexity of pensions, income protection and health policies means they cannot be sold like vehicle and property cover. The individuals' demands differ too much and products must be specifically tailored.
Virgin Group, owned by British entrepreneur Richard Branson, challenged this attitude with the launch last month of a low-cost personal pension product sold over the telephone.
Commercial Union, the large composite insurer, has set up a British-based life tele-sales operation, which commenced dealing in May.
RBS has not disclosed the price of the Scottish Equitable transaction and declined to comment on the value of the proposed deal with Scottish Widows.

Shares in RBS rose 4-1/2 pence to 4.93 pounds ($8.19) by 1155 GMT. Analysts said the proposed venture with Widows was a positive move, but was unlikely to have an immediate impact on profitability or drive the share price much higher in the short term.
